meta.title: AGENTS.md or a skill?
meta.goal: After this you can decide whether a piece of guidance belongs in AGENTS.md or in a skill, and say why in one sentence.

criterion.text: Get 6 of the 7 graded steps right, including which file rides along on every turn.

steps.hint: Two things arrive for every request: the project's own instruction files, and one line for each skill you have installed.
steps.prompt: Turn 1 asks something your skill has nothing to do with. What is still sitting in the model's context?
options: The whole of AGENTS.md, and the skill's name and description
The whole of AGENTS.md, and nothing at all from the skill
The whole of AGENTS.md, the skill's description, and the skill's body
steps.feedback: AGENTS.md is carried in full on every turn, because it is part of the instructions the session opens with. A skill is carried as one line, its name and description, and that line is what the model matches your request against. The body stays on disk until the line matches.

misconception.1: It feels like a skill you have not used yet is invisible. One line of each installed skill is in the list the model reads at the start, and that line is the whole reason a skill can fire on its own.
misconception.2: The description is loaded. The body is not. The model reads the body only after it decides the skill is relevant, which is the point of splitting the two.
misconception.default: One line per skill is always loaded. The body waits.

steps.hint: Watch the top shelf and the bottom shelf as the turns go by.
steps.prompt: Six turns in a row, and only turn 4 is a request the skill is for. Drag the slider and watch what each shelf carries.

widget.caption: Every turn pays for the whole of AGENTS.md. The skill's body is paid for once, on the turn it is needed.

steps.prompt: Where does each line belong? Drag each one onto a side.

items.text: Never push to main. Open a pull request.
Our test command is npm test, and it must pass before you commit.
How to turn a topic into a ten step practice exercise.
Cite AI-written code with an inline comment.
The palette, the type scale and the spacing tokens for design work.
Write plainly, in short sentences, with no em dashes.
The eight steps for publishing a page to GitHub Pages.
Who to email when the build breaks.

steps.feedback: AGENTS.md holds the short things that have to be true on every turn: invariants, house voice, and one line facts like the test command or who to email. A skill holds the long things that only matter on some turns: a procedure, a checklist, a pile of reference. The test is not importance. It is whether the line has to hold on a turn about something else entirely.
steps.misconception: The tempting mistake is to file by importance, so a rule you care about becomes a skill. Importance is the wrong test. Ask instead whether the line has to hold on every turn, even a turn about something unrelated.

steps.hint: Think about what every turn pays for.
steps.prompt: Your AGENTS.md has reached 900 lines and the model has started missing rules that sit in the middle. What is the fix?
options: Move the long procedures and reference into skills, and keep the invariants in AGENTS.md
Repeat the rules you care about at the top and again at the bottom
Delete the rules the model has been ignoring, because it must not need them
steps.feedback: Every turn pays for the whole file, and a longer file pushes each rule further from the front of the model's attention. Repeating a rule costs that much more on every turn and makes the file longer again. Deleting the ignored ones guesses at the wrong cause: a rule is usually missed because of where it sits, not because it is wrong. Move what only matters sometimes into a skill, where the cost waits until it is needed.

misconception.1: Repetition feels like emphasis, and on a page it is. In a prompt it is more tokens carried on every turn, and it pushes the next rule further away.
misconception.2: Being ignored is not evidence that a rule is unwanted. A rule missed in the middle of a long file is usually in the wrong file, not in the wrong list.
misconception.default: The file is too long, not too weakly worded.

steps.prompt: Which of these should be skills the model may not start on its own, so only a person can invoke them?
options: Publish your exercise to a public web page
Wipe the local database and reseed it
Explain what a React hook is
Turn a topic into a practice exercise
steps.feedback: Reserve it for the step that is hard to undo, or that has to be your decision: publishing, wiping a database, rotating keys. Everything else is better left reachable by the model, because a skill that only fires when you name it is a skill that never helps while you are thinking about something else.

misconception.2: Explaining a concept is safe and reversible. Locking it behind your own memory buys nothing and costs you the moment you would have been helped.
misconception.3: Building an exercise is the ordinary work of the class, and it is meant to happen while you are working on a topic. Leave it reachable.
misconception.default: Locking too much is the tempting mistake. A skill the model cannot reach does nothing until you remember it exists.

steps.prompt: Match each problem to the move that fixes it.
lefts: A rule that must hold on every task, and it is sometimes missed
A 200 line procedure the agent needs twice a week
A skill that exists but never fires
A step that publishes or deletes, and must run only when you ask
rights: Make it a skill, so the cost waits until it fires
Put it in AGENTS.md, so it is there on every turn
Rewrite the description to say what it does and when to use it
steps.feedback: A rule that must always hold cannot depend on the model noticing it, so it belongs in AGENTS.md. A long procedure that only matters now and then is a skill, where its cost waits. A skill that never fires has a description problem: the description is the only part the model reads when it decides. Anything hard to undo, or that is your call, gets disable-model-invocation: true.
steps.misconception: A rule you must never miss feels like it needs a procedure behind it, so making it a skill is tempting. But a skill fires only when the model reads your request and decides it is relevant, and a rule that has to hold every time cannot wait for that.

steps.prompt: Put the four questions in the order that decides where a piece of guidance goes.
options: Then it is a skill. Does the model need to find it on its own?
Must this hold on every single task, with no exception?
If not, add disable-model-invocation: true so a person starts it.
Is it short enough to be worth carrying on every turn?
steps.feedback: Ask first whether the line has to be true on every turn, because that decides it. If it does, no skill can promise it, since a skill fires only when the model decides it is relevant. If it does not have to hold every turn, ask whether it is short. Short and occasional still fits in AGENTS.md. Anything longer becomes a skill, and the last question is whether the model should be able to reach for it on its own.
steps.misconception: It is tempting to start with whether the model should find it on its own, because that is the interesting question. But it is the last one. A line that must hold on every turn never reaches it, because no skill can promise that.

steps.prompt: A rule that must hold on every task belongs in which file? Type its name.
steps.feedback: AGENTS.md is the file the session opens with, so it sits in front of the model on every turn. A skill is the other shelf: one line always, and its body only on the turn that line matches.
steps.misconception: A skill is the wrong answer here, and it is the common one. A skill is reached only when the model decides the request is relevant, so it cannot promise that a rule holds on every turn.
